label: paragraph_title
text: CURSING MOB.

label: text
text: WUCHOW MISSIONARIES

label: text
text: Passage to Shore Cut

label: text
text: An organised attempt by the Strike pickets and others in Wuchow to obtain possession of the very fine hospital and school buildings there, run by the American Baptist Mission, was described to be "China Mall" representative this morning by Mr. Rex Ray who has been in charge in Wuchow and who arrived in Hongkong yesterday by the s.s. "Lungsham."

label: text
text: Life at Wuchow had become so impossible under the conditions precipitated by the strike pickets and the lack of protection by the police and military that the schools and hospitals have had to be closed down. Mr. Ray thinks, however, that the mission has defeated the ends of the pickets which he is convinced were that the hospital fixtures and staff should be taken over and run under Chinese administration.

label: text
text: Demands had, in fact, been presented to the hospital and school staff on March 23 that they should sign an agreement handling over all the property to a representative Chinese committee and on being met with refusal one of the leaders amongst the Chinese entered the hospital and stated that from that time, all the funds of the hospital were to be turned over to him. The comprudore was told that if he failed to comply he would be put to death. The intruder was removed but it was apparent that the movement was well organised and fairly widespread and that the mission would get no support from the police or military who stated openly that all they would afford was a safe transport from Wuchow to the mission staff.

label: text
text: An attempt was made to seize the girls' school but this also was defeated and it became apparent that there was nothing to do but to leave. Determined that the hospital and schools should not fall into the hands of the pickets and others who had set themselves out to make of it an entirely Chinese concern, arrangements were made by which the whole of the buildings were locked and sealed with the American seal.

label: text
text: The escape of the mission staff was made under difficulties. "All day long as we worked," stated Mr. Ray, a howling, cursing mob did all they could to interfere and annoy. In spite of assurances of police and military facilities for our departure, no labour for removal of the baggage was forthcoming. What is more, the mob were allowed to tear down the elevated train way that leads from the shore to the Sai Hing Company's floating pier where we were taking the baggage and from where the boat to Canton puts in. As I was on the pier at the time, together with Mr. Lang, we had to jump into the water, which was waist high, and wade ashore. I used a pole to vault over the deeper part."

label: text
text:
"During the last day, whilst the staff was moving the baggage out, some of the mob were throwing brick bats and knocking out the front windows of the dispensary of the hospital," continued Mr. Ray. "As this and the jeering was going on, one of the pickets said to them 'Don't keep on destroying the property as it will all be ours in a few days.'".
Mr. Ray is convinced, however, that the action of sealing up the locks with the American seal will effectively check any such action. The U.S.S. "Pampanga" is standing by.

label: text
text:
The trouble between the mission and the strike pickets dates back to the latter part of 1924 when it was discovered that a former teacher was making use of the Mission's book store to spread Bolshevik doctrines also to August, 1925 when the bookstore was found to be filled with hideous cartoons on the Shameen affair of June 23. These were torn down and the store closed and this was the beginning of the trouble.

label: text
text: A street sweeper was charged before Major C. Wilson at the Central Magistracy this morning with behaving in a disorderly manner and using insulting language at Mrs. E. Thompson, of 20, Humphreys Building, Kowloon, at Battery Path yesterday morning. In evidence Mrs. Thompson stated that she was going to church in a sedan chair when the coolie obstructed the way and pushed the lending chair coolie, nearly upsetting the chair. Witnesses then asked the accused to get out of the way and he used a bad expression in Chinese which she understood. Witness corrected a statement made by accused that the words complained of were used to the chair coolie by stating that the abuse was undoubtedly meant for her, as the words were applicable to a woman.

label: text
text: SETTLEMENT RUMOURS.

label: text
text: How even "in the ten-houses and restaurants" everybody in Canton is daily discussing the settlement of the boycott is related by Japanese correspondent who came down to Hongkong on the "Lung-shan" yesterday.

label: text
text: Speaking to the representative of a vernacular paper, the correspondent said that he had no private capacity) interviewed Mr. So Snuching (chairman of the Boycott and Strike Committee). Mr. So is quoted as having replied to the effect that the Political Commission of Government has already held one meeting when instructions were given to the workmen to bring about a quick settlement. Further than that, and as to what had been done, Mr. So would not say, added the correspondent, but Mr. So said that something would be known before long. The correspondent also said that the Canton public was hopeful and that there were persistent rumours of an early resumption of communication between Hongkong and Canton.

label: text
text: A local business man who came down on the same steamer is reported to have seen Mr. Lul King to (who took a large part in the settlement of the 1922 seamen's strike), but had nothing to say beyond the lack of reference in the Canton press to negotiations.

text:

label: paragraph_title
text: TURFING TALK

label: text
text: LOCAL EXPERTS "DO'S AND DON'T'S."

label: text
text: LITTLE KNOWN INDUSTRY.

label: text
text: Weather vagaries in Hongkong have a great bearing on the turf required for various purposes, necessitating a good deal of attention.

label: text
text: That the turfing industry is fairly extensive is evident from the fact that there are experts who have been constantly engaged in it.

label: text
text: Many think that the Chinese gardener is the only person who does turfing jobs. This is not the case. Mr. Yeung Wing-hong, principal of Messrs. Yeung Fat (Fat Lee), of No. 69, Wanehal Road, who has kindly supplied the information to the "China Mail," has been a student at the Hongkong University. His firm have been contractors to the Botanical and Forestry Department for many years.

label: text
text: Nearly all the "material" used in the Colony comes from the New Territories, from places like Sal Kong and Un Long where there are unlimited supplies.

label: text
text: The workmen have been brought up in the trade—like every other Chinese artisan—by experience and are specialists.

label: text
text: First of all, the ground—whether it is a tennis court or garden lawn—must be “loosened” and well raked. If the soil is not suitable, then black soil must be used; this being obtainable (on the surface) from the Peak and other places. Black soil has nutritive effects on grass. It is used, the turfing may last for several years; if not, the “life” is appreciably shortened, but it all depends on the nature of the soil. The ground may be “too salty,” or the siting may be shaded by trees (or buildings) which prevent the grass, making sufficient sunlight. In such cases, “repairs” may be needed after a year, or longer.

label: text
text: How It Is Done.

label: text
text: Turf is taken about in sods of from 10 to 14 inches square. Mixed up with earth, each piece is about 1½ to 2 inches thick. It has to be well beaten down with a wooden hammer, in case the ground is not uniformly loose. Each sod overlaps its neighbours to ensure a good "fit." Otherwise, in dry weather there is contraction and cracks appear.

label: text
text: Spring is the best season to pu in turfing and autumn the mos unfavourable.

label: text
text: Workmen who dig up the turf are also employed in laying it down where wanted. They dig to a certain depth with spades and shovel up each sod in a stereotyped way.

label: text
text: For a plot of about 400 or 500 square yards (which would be the area of the average tennis court), the price would be from 40 to 45 cents per square yard on the upper levels, and from 80 to 40 cents a square yard for Kowloon and the lower levels. Such rates do not include the expense of raking or black soil, as these items must be dealt with according to requirements.

label: text
text: Mr. Young advises: Do not roll immediately after turf is laid. Give it a chance to sink in and for the roots of the grass to grow. For tennis courts, one should wait till the grass has grown and is rolled three or more times, before there should be any cutting. How long turf takes to be firmly embedded depends on the weather and the soil.

label: text

label: text
text: [By "Li Chung-yin](http://www.by-lin.edu.cn)

label: text
text: keep pets or other animals? And how many know what are the responsibilities entitled?

label: text
text:
There has been no tiger "scare" for some time. But Peak residents motoring to town have spotted a strange animal, a monkey has escaped, and dog-owners are thinking about the law now that there is an outbreak of rabies.
One cannot trot out a performing box constrictor or tame baby elephant, anywhere, with impunity. The law is very distinct on the subject.

label: text
text: There is that "famous local Ordinance—No. 1 of 1845—which degals with a multitude of sins. It is" designed, "An Ordinance to make provision for the preservation of Good Order, of Cleanliness and the prevention of Nuisances." Section 3 starts with "Every person shall be liable to a fine of not exceeding $50 who in any thoroughfare or public place adjacent thereto, commits any of the following offences":—

label: text
text: Each sub-section sets out a long list of offences but it is No. 9 that meets the eye. Inter-alla, it says:

label: text
text: cleans, dresses, exercises, trains or breaks any horse or other animal.

label: text
text:
Why, any special mention of a horse should be made is a matter for conjecture, but the general purport is plain enough. Beyond this any person can always take civil action for damages. The domestic. A jury, or a judge in the position of a jury, would vary likely deem that the owner of a non-domestic animal was causing unnecessary danger to the public by bringing it out and as every person keeps an animal at his own penal, it is supposed that damages will be awarded.
I am not referring to any specific instance. Each case, I suppose, is dealt with on its merits. Many strange things happen and I recall the fact that the famous "Peak tiger" was supposed to have escaped from captivity in Hongkong. That tiger was ultimately shot in the New Territories, but not till it had killed a European police sergeant, and at least one other police officer.

label: text
text: PRESIDENT AND LEAGUE OF NATIONS

label: text
text: CONGRESS CLOSED

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: The Argentine Congress having failed to act on the Presidential message recommending Argentine's adherence to the League of Nations, the Government will determine its course at the forthcoming Cabinet Council. It is believed that it will take the matter in its own hands and appoint delegates to the preparatory Disarmament Conference and the League Council Reconstruction Commission.

label: text
text: The message was withdrawn by a Presidential decree closing the Congress on the ground that the Deputies had failed to take up a single item laid before them since November.

label: text
text: The decreed has caused a stir in Parliamentary circles. Several Deputies have denounced it as a blow against the liberty of the people, whilst it is asserted that the Chamber has always been ready to do its duty, but could not accept Government imposition and dictation.

label: text
text: General Feng Yu-hsiang (the Christian general) has sent a delegate to Canton to report on the latest conditions of the North as well as to negotiate plans for the unification of the whole of China. The representative is Mr. Ma Pak-yan who is stated to have arrived at Canton with Mr. Sun To on March 30.
